issues.legal_issue: A landlord who has retired before receiving a demand to vacate authority-allotted residential accommodation may still qualify for the special right to recover possession if the statutory conditions are met.
material_facts: The landlord had occupied residential accommodation allotted by the government and owned a residential property in the territory.
The government required him to vacate the allotted accommodation because he owned that property, but he had retired before receiving the demand.
He sought possession of the property let to the tenant under the special recovery procedure.
issues.conclusion: Retirement before the demand to vacate did not disqualify the landlord from the benefit of section 14A.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14A(1) speaks of a landlord who is a person occupying residential premises allotted by the Central Government or a local authority and required to vacate them because of ownership of residential accommodation; it does not limit the right to serving government employees. The word “person” must be given its plain meaning where the statutory wording is precise and unambiguous. The Court referred to Nihal Chand v. Kalyan Chand Jain, [1978] 2 SCR 183, while explaining the issue of retirement.

rule.if: special_eviction_case and landlord_occupied_authority_allotted_residence and landlord_owned_residential_home and landlord_required_to_vacate_because_of_owned_home and landlord_retired_before_vacate_demand

predicates.special_eviction_case: The landlord brought a proceeding seeking recovery of let premises under a special procedure for persons required to leave authority-allotted residential accommodation.
predicates.landlord_occupied_authority_allotted_res: The landlord occupied residential accommodation allotted to the landlord by a public authority.
predicates.landlord_owned_residential_home: The landlord owned residential accommodation in the relevant territory.
predicates.landlord_required_to_vacate_because_of_o: A public authority required the landlord to vacate the allotted accommodation because the landlord owned residential accommodation.
predicates.landlord_retired_before_vacate_demand: The landlord retired before the public authority demanded that the landlord vacate the allotted accommodation.

issues.definition: When a landlord in a special recovery proceeding meets the stated allotment, ownership and vacating-demand conditions, retirement before that demand does not prevent eligibility.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord proceeding under the special recovery provision need not show that the let premises were let solely for residential use.
material_facts: The premises had been constructed for residential purposes.
The lease permitted residential and professional use, and the tenant used the premises on that basis.
The landlord sought possession under the special recovery provision.
issues.conclusion: The mixed residential and professional use did not prevent the landlord from seeking possession under section 14A; the premises did not have to have been let for residential purposes alone.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14A(1) refers to residential accommodation owned by the landlord and permits recovery of any premises let by the landlord; unlike section 14(1)(e), it does not require that the premises sought to be recovered were let for residential purposes. The Court referred to Busching Schmitz Private Ltd. v. P. T. Menghani, [1977] 3 SCR 312, and discussed Dr. Gopal Dass Verma v. Dr. S. K. Bhardwaj, [1962] 2 SCR 678, and Kartar Singh v. Chaman Lal, [1970] 1 SCR 9, in distinguishing the residential-letting requirement applicable under the ordinary ground.

predicates.special_eviction_case: The landlord brought a proceeding seeking recovery of let premises under the special procedure for persons required to leave authority-allotted residential accommodation.
predicates.landlord_meets_special_recovery_conditio: The landlord occupied authority-allotted residential accommodation, owned residential accommodation, and was required to vacate the allotted accommodation because of that ownership.
predicates.premises_intended_for_residential_accomm: The premises sought to be recovered were intended or constructed for residential accommodation.
predicates.premises_let_for_residential_and_profess: The landlord let the premises for both residential and professional use.

issues.definition: In a special recovery proceeding, premises intended for residential accommodation are not excluded merely because they were let for both residential and professional use.

issues.legal_issue: A pending earlier eviction proceeding on a different ground does not bar a later proceeding based on the special recovery right.
material_facts: The landlord had an earlier eviction petition pending against the tenant.
The later petition relied on the special right arising from the landlord's occupation of authority-allotted accommodation and the requirement to vacate it.
The earlier petition relied on different grounds.
issues.conclusion: The pending earlier petition did not prevent the landlord from bringing the special recovery proceeding.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14A confers a distinct right based on circumstances different from the grounds in the earlier petition; the earlier proceeding therefore did not bar the later petition.

predicates.special_eviction_case: The landlord brought a proceeding seeking recovery of let premises under the special procedure for persons required to leave authority-allotted residential accommodation.
predicates.earlier_eviction_case_pending: A proceeding seeking eviction of the same tenant from the premises was already pending.
predicates.earlier_and_later_cases_have_different_b: The earlier proceeding relied on grounds different from the special right relied on in the later proceeding.

issues.definition: A pending earlier eviction case on a different basis does not bar a later special recovery case.

issues.legal_issue: Leave to contest a special recovery application may be granted only when the tenant's affidavit discloses facts that would disentitle the landlord from obtaining possession on the special ground.
material_facts: The tenant sought leave to contest the landlord's special recovery application.
The tenant raised objections concerning the landlord's status after retirement, the pending earlier petition, and the premises' mixed residential and professional use.
The Court held that the statutory grounds for leave were confined to facts capable of defeating the landlord's entitlement under the special recovery provision.
issues.conclusion: The scope of leave under section 25B(5) is restricted to cases where the tenant's affidavit discloses facts that would disentitle the landlord from obtaining possession under section 14A.
issues.legal_principle: Section 25B(5) requires leave where the tenant's affidavit discloses facts that would disentitle the landlord from recovery on the applicable statutory ground. For a section 14A application, the relevant facts are those negating the landlord's entitlement under that section, such as the required occupation or the qualifying order to vacate. This restricted test is not analogous to leave to defend under Order XXXVII, Rule 2(3), and Rule 3(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.special_eviction_case: The landlord brought a proceeding seeking recovery of let premises under the special procedure for persons required to leave authority-allotted residential accommodation.
predicates.tenant_affidavit_discloses_facts_negatin: The tenant's affidavit stated facts which, if established, would defeat the landlord's entitlement to recover possession under the special ground.

issues.definition: In a special recovery proceeding, leave to contest must be granted when the tenant's affidavit states facts that would defeat the landlord's eligibility for recovery under that ground.

issues.legal_issue: The ordinary restriction based on the period since acquisition of the premises does not apply to a landlord who qualifies for the special recovery right.
material_facts: The landlord sought possession under the special recovery provision and met its qualifying conditions.
The tenant argued that the restrictions associated with the ordinary residential-need ground also had to be satisfied.
The Court held that the special provision, as read with the applicable procedural provision, displaced the acquisition-period restriction for qualifying landlords.
issues.conclusion: A qualifying landlord proceeding under section 14A is not subject to the five-year acquisition restriction in section 14(6).
issues.legal_principle: Section 14(6) restricts recovery on the ordinary ground in section 14(1)(e) where the landlord acquired the premises by transfer within the specified period. Section 25C(1) makes that restriction inapplicable to a landlord who fulfils section 14A(1). The requirements of section 14(1)(e) therefore need not be imported into a section 14A application.

predicates.special_eviction_case: The landlord brought a proceeding seeking recovery of let premises under the special procedure for persons required to leave authority-allotted residential accommodation.
predicates.landlord_meets_special_recovery_conditio: The landlord occupied authority-allotted residential accommodation, owned residential accommodation, and was required to vacate the allotted accommodation because of that ownership.
predicates.premises_acquired_within_ordinary_restri: The landlord acquired the premises within the period that would restrict recovery under the ordinary residential-need ground.

issues.definition: A landlord meeting the conditions for special recovery is not barred by the ordinary acquisition-period restriction, even if the premises were acquired within that period.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord obtaining a possession order under the special recovery provision must wait the shortened post-order period before taking possession.
material_facts: The landlord sought an order under the special recovery provision.
The tenant argued that the ordinary restrictions on recovery, including the post-order waiting requirement, did not apply to that proceeding.
The Court held that the procedural provision expressly applied a shortened post-order waiting period to special recovery proceedings.
issues.conclusion: Even a landlord proceeding under section 14A must wait two months from the possession order before obtaining possession.
issues.legal_principle: Section 25C(2) applies to orders made under both section 14(1)(e) and section 14A and substitutes two months for the six-month period in section 14(7). Unlike the acquisition restriction in section 14(6), this post-order waiting requirement applies to a special recovery order.

predicates.special_eviction_case: The landlord brought a proceeding seeking recovery of let premises under the special procedure for persons required to leave authority-allotted residential accommodation.
predicates.possession_order_granted: The decision-maker granted an order for recovery of possession in the special recovery proceeding.

issues.definition: When a possession order is granted in a special recovery proceeding, the landlord must wait the applicable shortened post-order period before taking possession.
